opus-5.5.text:
I think there's actually a really interesting asymmetry there. With AI assistants, language models, a lot of the supervision is very rich up front. You pretrain on enormous amounts of human-written text, and then you do some fine-tuning and some RLHF on top of that. But when the model makes a mistake in a conversation, the consequences are pretty soft. Maybe the user rephrases the question, maybe they give a thumbs down, and that signal is noisy and indirect. It's hard to close the loop.

In robotics, the situation is kind of flipped. We don't have the internet-scale corpus of robot data to pretrain on, so we start from a much poorer place in terms of demonstrations. But when a robot makes a mistake, it's very concrete. It drops the cup, it fails to fold the shirt, the object falls on the floor. The physical world gives you very clear feedback. And critically, the robot can often recover. It can pick the thing back up, try again, and see what works. That's a very natural setting for learning from experience, for reinforcement learning, in a way that's actually harder to set up cleanly for a chatbot.

So I think what we're seeing is that robotics is borrowing the first part from language models: use these big pretrained vision-language models as a foundation, so the robot starts out with a lot of common sense about the world. Then the second part, where it learns from its own mistakes in deployment, might actually be where robotics gets ahead in some ways. Embodied agents get grounded, unambiguous feedback, and if you can build systems that improve autonomously from that, that's a really powerful flywheel.

And I'd go further and say that this is something AI assistants will eventually need too. Right now they're mostly imitating people. To go beyond human performance, they'll need to learn from the outcomes of their own actions, and in a sense, robotics is a place where we're forced to confront that problem head-on, because there's no shortcut. You can't just scrape the web for robot data. You have to actually interact with the world and learn from what happens.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that people cooperating with a robot are motivated to supervise it because they want the task to succeed.

r002.rationale: It says a robot can recover by picking an object back up and trying again, and contrasts this with the harder-to-close feedback loop for a chatbot.

r003.rationale: It describes robot mistakes as concrete with clear feedback, while assistant feedback is soft, noisy, and indirect.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most interesting asymmetries between the two settings. With AI assistants, the supervision is really dense in a certain sense. You have people typing questions, you have thumbs up and thumbs down, you have comparisons, and the whole system is embedded in a loop with millions of users where every interaction is potentially a signal. And the mistakes are cheap. If the assistant says something wrong, the user corrects it or just ignores it and moves on. Nothing breaks.

Robotics is almost the opposite on both counts. The supervision is expensive because somebody has to physically demonstrate the task, or set up the environment, or stand there and watch the robot and intervene. And the mistakes are expensive too. If the robot drops the glass, the glass is broken. If it pushes too hard on the drawer, maybe the drawer is broken. So you can't just let it flail around and collect a billion interactions the way you can with text.

But I actually think the robotics setting has an advantage that's underappreciated, which is that the feedback is much more grounded. When a language model makes a mistake, figuring out that it was a mistake often requires a person to judge it, and people are inconsistent and sometimes wrong. When a robot makes a mistake, the world tells you. The object didn't move. The cup is on the floor. The task didn't get done. That's a signal that doesn't depend on anybody's opinion, and it's a signal you can get autonomously if you set things up right.

So the way I think about it, the assistant setting has solved the problem of scale but has a kind of noisy, subjective reward, and the robotics setting has a clean, physical reward but hasn't solved scale. And a lot of what I'm excited about is trying to get the robotics side closer to the scale regime, where you have robots out in the world doing real things, and every time one of them succeeds or fails at something, that experience gets folded back into the model. Once you have that loop, learning from mistakes in robotics could actually be more effective than it is for assistants, because the mistakes are so unambiguous.

The hard part, honestly, is the beginning. You need the robot to be good enough that letting it try things is worthwhile and not just destructive. That's where the demonstrations and the pretraining on diverse data come in. You bootstrap to competence, and then the real learning starts.

r001.rationale: The response says robot supervision is costly because people must demonstrate, set up, watch, or intervene. It does not say they are motivated by wanting the task to succeed.

r002.rationale: It describes physical mistakes as costly and potentially destructive, but does not say robot tasks offer more opportunities to recover from mistakes than assistant interactions.

r003.rationale: It says the world makes robot mistakes clear—for example, an object not moving or a cup falling—while judging an assistant’s mistake often requires a person.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s an interesting difference in how easy it is to get supervision, versus how easy it is to know that you made a mistake.

For an AI assistant, it’s relatively easy for a person to provide an example of what they should do. You can write a good answer, or look at two answers and say which one you prefer. With a robot, providing a demonstration can be quite cumbersome. You might need to teleoperate it, and the person has to figure out how to control this particular machine.

But sometimes the situation reverses when you ask whether the system succeeded. If a robot tries to pick up an object and drops it, there’s a physical outcome that it can observe. If an assistant gives you advice about a complicated decision, it might be very difficult to determine whether that advice was actually good. Getting a thumbs-up from the user doesn’t necessarily resolve that.

Of course, the robot’s mistakes can also be costly. You want it to learn from trying things, but you don’t want every learning experience to involve breaking something. So the challenge is to give it enough initial competence that it can practice safely, and then use the outcomes of its own actions to improve. That ability to learn from experience, beyond just copying demonstrations, is something I think is important for both robotics and assistants.

r001.rationale: The response says robot demonstrations can be cumbersome, but does not say people are motivated to supervise because they want the task to succeed.

r002.rationale: It contrasts how readily success can be assessed, but does not state that physical robot tasks offer more opportunities to recover from mistakes than answering questions.

r003.rationale: It says a robot dropping an object has an observable physical outcome, while it can be difficult to tell whether an assistant’s advice was good.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s an interesting trade-off. With an AI assistant, it’s relatively easy to provide supervision: a person can read an answer and say whether it’s good, or demonstrate a better answer. In robotics, providing a demonstration can be much more cumbersome. You might need to teleoperate the robot, and even then it’s hard to communicate exactly how it should move.

But robots have an advantage when it comes to learning from their own mistakes. If a robot tries to pick something up and drops it, the physical world provides a fairly concrete signal that something went wrong. If an assistant gives you advice, it may never observe whether that advice actually helped. It mostly observes whether you liked the answer, which isn’t necessarily the same thing.

Of course, the robot’s mistakes can be expensive, and recognizing success isn’t always simple. But I think that distinction matters: how easy is it to tell the system what to do, versus how easy is it for the system to try something and find out whether it worked?

r001.rationale: The response discusses how cumbersome robot supervision can be, but does not say people are motivated to provide it because they want the task to succeed.

r002.rationale: It says robots can learn from concrete signals after mistakes, but does not state that physical tasks offer more opportunities to recover than answering questions.

r003.rationale: It contrasts a dropped object as a concrete signal of failure with an assistant that may not observe whether its advice helped.
